item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the passage's characterization of microcredit's benefit?
choices: Households that received microloans started markedly more new businesses than otherwise similar households that received no loans.
Microloan borrowers reported greater trust in formal financial institutions after repayment, and were likelier than non-borrowers to open a savings account.
Regions served by many microfinance institutions had lower overall poverty rates a decade later than otherwise similar regions where such lenders stayed scarce.
Borrowers with microloans were no more likely than non-borrowers to raise their annual income but were better able to cover irregular, lumpy expenses.
item.passage: Microfinance was heralded as a tool for lifting the poor out of poverty by extending small business loans to those whom banks ignore. Rigorous evaluations have tempered that promise. Across randomized trials, access to microcredit rarely raised household income or consumption and seldom expanded businesses beyond subsistence scale. Yet the studies converge on a subtler benefit: borrowers gained flexibility in the timing of their spending, smoothing consumption across lean and flush periods and financing lumpy purchases they could not otherwise have afforded. The value of microcredit, the evidence suggests, lies not in generating new wealth but in rearranging the wealth households already have across time—a real service, though not the transformative engine of enterprise its champions once described.
item.explanation: The passage's specific claim is that microcredit rearranges wealth across time rather than creating it, so the finding that borrowers 'were no more likely than non-borrowers to raise their annual income but were better able to cover irregular, lumpy expenses' matches both halves of that claim at once. The finding that microloan households 'started markedly more new businesses' would support the engine-of-enterprise view the passage explicitly sets aside. The finding that borrowers 'reported greater trust in formal financial institutions' after repayment is plausible but has nothing to do with the timing of spending. And the finding that regions with many lenders 'had lower overall poverty rates a decade later' is a region-level claim about wealth creation, not the household-level smoothing the passage endorses.
item.correct_answer: Borrowers with microloans were no more likely than non-borrowers to raise their annual income but were better able to cover irregular, lumpy expenses.

distractor_rationales.choice: Households that received microloans started markedly more new businesses than otherwise similar households that received no loans.
Microloan borrowers reported greater trust in formal financial institutions after repayment, and were likelier than non-borrowers to open a savings account.
Regions served by many microfinance institutions had lower overall poverty rates a decade later than otherwise similar regions where such lenders stayed scarce.

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the author's characterization of the shift to agriculture?
choices: Some forager groups living beside farming villages declined to take up agriculture for many centuries.
The earliest farming settlements were far larger and more densely settled than the forager camps that preceded them on the same land.
Skeletons from the first farming communities show greater height and fewer stress markers than neighboring foragers'.
Early crops delivered several times more calories per acre than the wild foods gathered from the same land.
item.passage: The transition to agriculture is routinely narrated as an obvious upgrade: farming produced more food, so foragers naturally adopted it. Skeletal evidence complicates the story. The bones of early farmers show, relative to the foragers who preceded them, shorter stature, more dental disease, and more markers of nutritional stress—hardly the profile of a population that had traded up. Agriculture did yield more calories per acre, but those calories came from a narrower range of starchy staples, purchased with longer labor and denser settlement that bred infection. Why, then, did anyone farm? The likeliest answer is not that farming was better but that, once populations had grown around it, returning to foraging could no longer feed them. Agriculture may have been less a prize that foragers seized than a trap that closed behind them—advantageous to the group's numbers even as it diminished the individual's health.
item.explanation: The author's characterization is that farming was a trap: good for the group's numbers, bad for the individuals, with the skeletal record supplying the evidence of that individual cost. Skeletons from the first farming communities showing "greater height and fewer stress markers than neighboring foragers" would reverse that evidence and pull the load-bearing support out from under the claim. The strongest trap is the finding that early crops "delivered several times more calories per acre" than wild foods - it feels like a refutation, but the passage already concedes the caloric advantage and denies that it translated into individual well-being. The observation that the earliest farming settlements "were far larger and more densely settled" than the camps before them fits the argument, since denser settlement is one of the costs the author names. And the fact that some forager groups "declined to take up agriculture for many centuries" bears on how fast farming spread, not on whether farmers were healthier.
item.correct_answer: Skeletons from the first farming communities show greater height and fewer stress markers than neighboring foragers'.

distractor_rationales.choice: Some forager groups living beside farmers declined to adopt agriculture for many centuries.
The earliest farming settlements were larger and more densely populated than forager camps.
Early crops delivered more calories per acre than the wild foods gathered from the same land.

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the skeptic's hypothesis?
choices: Large, pre-registered studies find little or no bilingual advantage, while the positive results cluster among smaller studies.
Bilingual adults outperform monolingual adults on some attention tasks but not on others, with the gap appearing mainly on tasks that demand rapid switching.
Children who begin a second language earlier show larger executive-function advantages than those who begin later, a dose-response pattern across ages.
Monolingual children can improve their executive function through several weeks of targeted attention training.
item.passage: Bilingual children are frequently said to enjoy a general "executive-function advantage"—better attention control and task-switching—attributed to the constant effort of managing two languages. Early studies reported such advantages, but a skeptic notes that these findings came disproportionately from small samples and were more likely to be published when the effect was positive. She hypothesizes that the reported advantage is inflated by this publication filter rather than reflecting a robust cognitive difference, and predicts a specific signature in the literature if she is right.
item.explanation: The skeptic blames a publication filter that favors positive results from small samples, and she predicts a specific signature in the literature. The finding that 'large, pre-registered studies find little or no bilingual advantage, while the positive results cluster among smaller studies' is precisely that signature: the effect appears where the filter can operate and vanishes where it cannot. The finding that bilingual adults 'outperform monolingual adults on some attention tasks but not on others' describes a patterned real effect, not an artifact of what gets published. The finding that 'children who begin a second language earlier show' larger advantages than late starters is a dose-response pattern, which points toward a genuine cognitive difference and cuts against her. And the finding that monolinguals 'can improve their executive function through several weeks' of training concerns a different question entirely.
item.correct_answer: Large, pre-registered studies find little or no bilingual advantage, while the positive results cluster among smaller studies.

distractor_rationales.choice: Bilingual adults outperform monolingual adults on some attention tasks but not on others, with the gap appearing mainly on tasks that demand rapid switching.
Children who begin a second language earlier show larger executive-function advantages than those who begin later, a dose-response pattern across ages.
Monolingual children can improve their executive function through several weeks of targeted attention training.

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the revisionist claim that the return of the wolves was not sufficient to produce the vegetation recovery?
choices: Elk populations fell sharply in the years immediately after wolves were reintroduced.
Beaver colonies increased across much of the park following the reintroduction of wolves.
Wolves hunted elk most successfully in the open bottoms of river valleys, where the browsing herds had few routes of escape.
Willow stands failed to recover where water tables were low, despite a heavy and sustained wolf presence.
item.passage: The reintroduction of wolves to Yellowstone has become the textbook illustration of a trophic cascade: with wolves back, elk abandon the exposed streamside groves where they are easily ambushed, browsing pressure eases, and willows and aspen surge back along the banks. Recent fieldwork, however, has questioned how clean the story really is. Willow recovery across the park has proved distinctly patchy. It has been vigorous where beaver dams raise the water table and keep the banks wet, and feeble or absent where those conditions are lacking—even in places where wolves are plainly present and elk are plainly wary. The predators' return, this work suggests, may well be a necessary ingredient of the recovery credited to it, but it is just as plainly not a sufficient one.
item.explanation: The revisionist point is that wolves are necessary but not sufficient — recovery also needs the right hydrology. The finding that 'willow stands failed to recover where water tables were low, despite a heavy and sustained wolf presence' is the direct demonstration: predation is at full strength and the vegetation still does not come back, so predation alone cannot be doing the work. The finding that 'elk populations fell sharply in the years immediately after wolves were reintroduced' is the tempting wrong answer, because it supports the classic cascade rather than the revisionist qualification of it. The finding that 'beaver colonies increased across much of the park' fits either story and so distinguishes neither. And the finding that wolves 'hunted elk most successfully in the open bottoms' of river valleys describes hunting behavior, which says nothing about whether predation suffices for willow recovery.
item.correct_answer: Willow stands failed to recover where water tables were low, despite a heavy and sustained wolf presence.

distractor_rationales.choice: Elk populations fell sharply in the years immediately after wolves were reintroduced.
Beaver colonies increased across much of the park following the reintroduction of wolves.
Wolves hunted elk most successfully in the open bottoms of river valleys.

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the passage's central claim?
choices: Evidence that a program meeting the classic conditions—equal status, shared goals, institutional support—sharply reduced participants' bias
A finding that reductions in prejudice from contact tend to fade once participants leave the structured setting
A large study showing that people who merely lived alongside an out-group, with no shared goals or institutional support, developed durably lower prejudice
A study showing that contact under unequal, competitive conditions increased hostility between groups
item.passage: The idea that bringing hostile groups into contact will erode their prejudices has an appealing simplicity, and decades of studies confirm that contact often does reduce bias. The finding is real; the simplicity is deceptive. Early researchers were explicit that contact helps only when certain conditions hold—when the groups meet as equals, pursue shared goals, and act with institutional support. Absent these, contact can as easily entrench hostility as dissolve it, as anyone who has watched rival factions share cramped quarters can attest. Later analyses complicate the picture further: some of the prejudice-reducing effect appears to spread to group members never actually encountered, while some evaporates once the structured setting is left behind. The evidence thus supports a claim narrower than the slogan—that contact of a particular, engineered kind reliably reduces prejudice—and warns against the broader inference that mere exposure will do the work on its own.
item.explanation: The central claim is that only engineered contact reliably works and mere exposure will not; durable bias reduction from unstructured proximity directly contradicts that. Options one and four both support the passage (structured contact works; unstructured contact backfires). The fading-effect finding also matches the passage's own qualification. Only the mere-exposure result undercuts the 'engineered kind' thesis.
item.correct_answer: A large study showing that people who merely lived alongside an out-group, with no shared goals or institutional support, developed durably lower prejudice

distractor_rationales.choice: Evidence that a program meeting the classic conditions—equal status, shared goals, institutional support—sharply reduced participants' bias
A finding that reductions in prejudice from contact tend to fade once participants leave the structured setting
A study showing that contact under unequal, competitive conditions increased hostility between groups

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the reconsideration described in the text?
choices: Children who waited longer for the treat scored higher on personality measures of conscientiousness years later, and the association held even after researchers adjusted for how stable the child's household had been.
Older children, on average, waited longer for the delayed reward than younger children did, and the difference widened with each additional year of age.
Children raised in households with unpredictable access to food waited less than peers from stable households, even when the two groups scored equally on independent tests of self-control.
Children who had just watched the experimenter break a promise waited as long for the second treat as children who had watched her keep one, whatever the stability of the household they came from.
item.passage: The famous 'marshmallow test'—in which young children who resisted an immediate treat for a larger delayed one later showed better life outcomes—is widely read as evidence that self-control is a stable trait that shapes a child's future. A reconsideration questions the direction of the lesson. Waiting, researchers point out, is only rational when the promise of a reward is credible; a child who has learned that adults' assurances often go unmet acts sensibly by taking the sure thing now. When experimenters first demonstrated that they were reliable, children waited far longer, and when they proved unreliable, previously 'patient' children grabbed the treat at once. On this reading, the test may measure not willpower but a child's evidence-based expectation about whether the world keeps its promises—an expectation that tracks the stability of the environment the child comes from.
item.explanation: The reconsideration recasts waiting as an evidence-based expectation about whether promises are kept, tracking the child's environment rather than a fixed trait. The finding that children from 'households with unpredictable access to food waited less' while the two groups 'scored equally on independent tests of self-control' holds willpower constant and lets environment alone move the waiting, which is the cleanest possible support. The finding that longer waiters 'scored higher on personality measures of conscientiousness years later,' with the association surviving adjustment for household stability, supports the stable-trait reading the passage is questioning. The observation that 'older children, on average, waited longer for the delayed reward' reflects maturation and does not separate a trait from an expectation. And the result that children who 'had just watched the experimenter break a promise waited as long' as those who saw one kept would actually weaken the reconsideration, since it says the reliability of promises makes no difference.
item.correct_answer: Children raised in households with unpredictable access to food waited less than peers from stable households, even when the two groups scored equally on independent tests of self-control.

distractor_rationales.choice: Children who waited longer for the treat scored higher on personality measures of conscientiousness years later, and the association held even after researchers adjusted for how stable the child's household had been.
Older children, on average, waited longer for the delayed reward than younger children did, and the difference widened with each additional year of age.
Children who had just watched the experimenter break a promise waited as long for the second treat as children who had watched her keep one, whatever the stability of the household they came from.

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the author's alternative explanation of the wrasse's behavior?
choices: Wrasses try to remove marks placed on their own bodies even when the marks resemble nothing they encounter while cleaning other fish.
Cleaner wrasses are unusually quick to notice the small blemishes on the bodies of the fish they clean.
Cleaner wrasses spend more time in front of a mirror than other reef fish placed in the same tank do.
Apes and dolphins scrape at a marked spot far more consistently than cleaner wrasses do when the same mark test is administered to both.
item.passage: When a cleaner wrasse, marked with a colored spot, scraped its body against surfaces after seeing itself in a mirror, some researchers hailed the fish as self-aware, extending to it a capacity long reserved for apes and dolphins. Caution is warranted. Passing the mark test may show only that an animal can associate a mirror reflection with its own body, a sensorimotor achievement that need not involve any concept of a self. The wrasse's ecology supplies a simpler reading: a fish whose living depends on detecting blemishes on other bodies might be primed to respond to a blemish wherever a reflection places it, with no inner spectator required. To infer rich self-awareness from the behavior is to assume that one impressive performance can be produced only by the most demanding mechanism—when a leaner one, well suited to the animal's way of life, will do.
item.explanation: The author's leaner explanation ties the wrasse's scraping to its ecology: a fish that makes its living spotting blemishes on other bodies is primed to react to a blemish wherever a reflection puts it. The finding that wrasses try to remove marks placed on their own bodies "even when the marks resemble nothing they encounter while cleaning other fish" breaks that link, because the response survives in cases the blemish-detection habit cannot explain, which reopens the richer self-awareness reading. The tempting wrong answer is that cleaner wrasses are "unusually quick to notice the small blemishes" on their clients: that reinforces the author's ecological account rather than weakening it. The option reporting that wrasses spend "more time in front of a mirror" than other reef fish records an attention difference that bears on curiosity, not on whether a self-concept is involved. And the comparison in which "apes and dolphins scrape at a marked spot" far more consistently than wrasses do may well be true, but a difference of degree across species leaves the author's proposed mechanism for the wrasse entirely intact.
item.correct_answer: Wrasses try to remove marks placed on their own bodies even when the marks resemble nothing they encounter while cleaning other fish.

distractor_rationales.choice: Cleaner wrasses are unusually quick to notice the small blemishes on the bodies of the fish they clean.
Cleaner wrasses spend more time in front of a mirror than other reef fish placed in the same tank do.
Apes and dolphins scrape at a marked spot far more consistently than cleaner wrasses do when the same mark test is administered to both.

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the author's argument?
choices: Across Europe the total number of books in circulation multiplied many times over within a few decades of the first printed editions.
In regions that adopted printing early, literacy rose sharply only generations later, once church-led schooling campaigns began.
Early printers competed fiercely for the trade in Latin editions of the classical authors.
Literacy rose fastest in the first decades after the press appeared, well before any schooling campaigns began.
item.passage: The printing press is celebrated as the engine of mass literacy, as though cheaper books had straightforwardly taught Europe to read. The chronology resists the compliment. For its first century and more, print largely served readers who already existed—clergy, jurists, merchants—and the commonest products of the early presses were not primers but liturgical works and learned tomes in Latin, a language most Europeans could not read at all. Literacy rates in many regions barely moved until the confessional campaigns and schooling drives of later centuries gave ordinary people both a reason to read and the instruction to do so. Print made those later expansions cheaper to sustain, but it did not by itself supply the motive or the teaching that literacy requires. The press was a necessary instrument of the reading public that eventually formed; it was not, on its own, the cause of that public's formation.
item.explanation: The argument is that the press was a necessary instrument but not the cause of mass literacy: early print served readers who already existed, mostly in Latin, and rates moved only when confessional campaigns and schooling supplied both motive and instruction. The finding that in early-printing regions "literacy rose sharply only generations later, once church-led schooling campaigns began" matches that chronology precisely and pins the rise on teaching rather than on the press. The trap is the finding that "the total number of books in circulation multiplied many times over" within a few decades - it measures printed volume, which the passage carefully separates from reading ability. The detail that early printers "competed fiercely for the trade in Latin editions" of the classical authors is consistent with the argument but establishes no causal timing, so it strengthens nothing. And the finding that literacy "rose fastest in the first decades after the press appeared," before any schooling campaigns, would contradict the argument outright.
item.correct_answer: In regions that adopted printing early, literacy rose sharply only generations later, once church-led schooling campaigns began.

distractor_rationales.choice: Across Europe the total number of books in circulation multiplied many times over within a few decades of the first printed editions.
Early printers competed fiercely for the trade in Latin editions of the classical authors.
Literacy rose fastest in the first decades after the press appeared, well before any schooling campaigns began.

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the carbon-dioxide hypothesis over the water hypothesis?
choices: The Martian gullies closely resemble the channels that seasonal runoff cuts in desert slopes on Earth.
Clay minerals that form only after prolonged exposure to liquid water have been identified in ancient terrain far from the gullies.
Time-lapse imaging shows gully material moving during the coldest months, when CO2 frost is present but liquid water cannot exist.
The gullies sit on slopes steep enough for loose debris to slide under gravity alone, without any lubricant.
item.passage: When narrow gullies were photographed on Martian crater walls, they were quickly read as the fingerprints of flowing water, and thus of a planet perhaps hospitable to life. The channels do resemble those water carves on Earth. But resemblance is not mechanism. Many of the gullies lie in places too cold for liquid water to persist, and their activity peaks not in the Martian summer but in the depths of winter, when carbon-dioxide frost accumulates and then sublimates. A growing number of planetary scientists therefore suspect the sculptor is not water at all but blocks of dry ice, lubricated by the gas they release as they slide. If so, the gullies say little about Mars's habitability.
item.explanation: The carbon-dioxide account depends on the gullies being active in winter, when CO2 frost sublimates and liquid water cannot persist. Time-lapse imaging showing gully material moving during the coldest months is exactly that discriminator: it fits sliding dry ice and excludes flowing water. The finding that the Martian gullies closely resemble the channels that seasonal runoff cuts in desert slopes on Earth is the trap - it leans toward the water reading, and the passage warns that 'resemblance is not mechanism.' The clay minerals that form only after prolonged exposure to liquid water are found in ancient terrain far from the gullies, so they speak to Mars's distant past, not to what carved these channels. And slopes steep enough for loose debris to slide under gravity alone would serve either agent equally, so that finding separates the two hypotheses not at all.
item.correct_answer: Time-lapse imaging shows gully material moving during the coldest months, when CO2 frost is present but liquid water cannot exist.

distractor_rationales.choice: The Martian gullies are shaped very similarly to water-cut channels found in deserts on Earth.
Mineral deposits requiring long exposure to liquid water are found elsewhere on Mars.
The gullies occur on slopes steep enough for loose material to slide under gravity alone.

item.prompt: Which observation would most support the mechanism described in the text?
choices: Average temperatures across Europe fell even as global average temperatures rose.
As freshwater flowing into the North Atlantic increased, the sinking of deep water slowed and the northward transport of heat weakened.
Greenland's ice sheet lost mass more rapidly during warmer years, shedding meltwater from its margins at rates that tracked each summer's temperatures.
Tropical ocean temperatures rose in step with the global average temperature.
item.passage: That a warming planet might make part of Europe colder sounds contradictory, yet it follows from the physics of ocean circulation. The Atlantic conveyor that carries tropical heat northward is driven partly by the sinking of cold, salty water in the far North Atlantic. As Greenland's ice melts, it floods that region with fresh water, which is less dense and sinks less readily; the circulation slows, and less tropical heat reaches northwestern Europe. The claim is carefully hedged. Researchers do not predict a new ice age, nor that regional cooling would offset global warming overall—the planet keeps warming. They argue only that a global mean temperature can conceal opposing regional trends, and that a warming world is compatible with, and could even produce, a cooler northwestern Europe.
item.explanation: The mechanism in the text is a three-link chain: meltwater freshens the far North Atlantic, fresher water sinks less readily, and the conveyor delivers less tropical heat northward. The observation that as freshwater inflow increased 'the sinking of deep water slowed and the northward transport of heat weakened' traces that chain link by link, which is why it is the strongest support. The observation that 'average temperatures across Europe fell even as global average temperatures rose' overstates a claim the passage carefully hedges, since the cooling is specific to northwestern Europe and the researchers deny that regional cooling offsets global warming. That 'Greenland's ice sheet lost mass more rapidly during warmer years' confirms the warming premise that starts the chain but says nothing about circulation. And that 'tropical ocean temperatures rose in step with the global average temperature' concerns the heat's source, not whether the conveyor still carries it north.
item.correct_answer: As freshwater flowing into the North Atlantic increased, the sinking of deep water slowed and the northward transport of heat weakened.

distractor_rationales.choice: Average temperatures across Europe fell even as global average temperatures rose.
Greenland's ice sheet lost mass more rapidly during warmer years.
Tropical ocean temperatures rose in step with the global average temperature.

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the author's central claim?
choices: A neighboring state that imported identical Western machinery but lacked comparable commercial institutions failed to industrialize at a similar pace.
The Meiji government spent more on foreign machinery than any other contemporaneous Asian state.
Foreign advisers in Japan were paid substantially higher salaries than they had earned at home, a premium that drew engineers and accountants to Meiji ministries.
Tokugawa-era literacy rates were significantly lower in rural regions than in major cities.
item.passage: Standard narratives attribute Japan's swift industrialization after 1868 to the Meiji government's importation of Western machinery and foreign advisers. The hardware mattered, but it does not explain why Japan absorbed what other nineteenth-century states could not. Long before Commodore Perry, Tokugawa Japan possessed high literacy, a dense commercial network, sophisticated rural proto-industry, and merchant houses skilled in double-entry accounting and futures trading. These endowments meant that imported technology met a workforce and a managerial class already primed to deploy it. Foreign experts were, tellingly, dismissed as soon as Japanese personnel could replace them—often within a decade. The Meiji reformers' genuine innovation lay less in acquiring foreign techniques than in redirecting indigenous capacities toward national ends. Where historians once read the period as a story of borrowing, the more defensible reading treats borrowing as the visible surface of a deeper continuity, one that the drama of Westernization has tended to obscure.
item.explanation: The thesis is that Japan absorbed Western technology because of indigenous endowments - high literacy, dense commercial networks, rural proto-industry, merchant houses skilled in accounting - rather than because of the imports themselves. A neighboring state that "imported identical Western machinery but lacked comparable commercial institutions" and still failed to industrialize holds the hardware constant while varying the institutions, isolating them as the decisive factor. The option that the Meiji government "spent more on foreign machinery than any other" contemporaneous Asian state measures the borrowing the author is demoting and says nothing about domestic capacity. The detail that advisers "were paid substantially higher salaries" than at home is true but idle here; what matters to the argument is how fast they were dismissed, not what they cost. And the finding that "literacy rates were significantly lower in rural regions" would chip away at the sophisticated rural proto-industry the author leans on, weakening the claim rather than strengthening it.
item.correct_answer: A neighboring state that imported identical Western machinery but lacked comparable commercial institutions failed to industrialize at a similar pace.

distractor_rationales.choice: The Meiji government spent more on foreign machinery than any other contemporaneous Asian state.
Foreign advisers in Japan were paid substantially higher salaries than they had earned at home.
Tokugawa-era literacy rates were significantly lower in rural regions than in major cities.

item.prompt: Which finding would most directly support the refined account over the popular version of the hygiene hypothesis?
choices: Children raised in unusually clean, nearly germ-free households had markedly higher rates of allergic disease than did children who grew up in ordinary, less sanitized homes.
Adults who contract frequent respiratory infections tend to have weaker immune systems overall than adults who rarely fall ill.
Children who suffered many ordinary childhood infections were no less allergic than those who suffered few, whereas children exposed to diverse environmental microbes were.
The 'old friend' microorganisms were far more common in the human environments of thousands of years ago than they are in the households of modern industrialized countries today.
item.passage: The 'hygiene hypothesis' is popularly summarized as a simple warning: modern cleanliness, by depriving children of germs, leaves their immune systems untrained and prone to allergy. Immunologists have largely abandoned that formulation. The rise in allergic disease does not correlate well with reduced exposure to the common infectious agents of childhood—colds, flus, and the like—which the crude version implicates. It correlates instead with diminished contact with a particular set of ancient, largely harmless microorganisms, the so-called 'old friends' that co-evolved with humans and help calibrate immune regulation. On this refined account, the problem is not insufficient infection but the loss of specific symbiotic exposures; a childhood full of ordinary colds confers little protection, while contact with the right environmental microbes does. Cleanliness is not quite the villain the slogan suggests.
item.explanation: The refined account's distinctive prediction is that ordinary childhood infections confer little protection while contact with specific 'old friend' microbes does. The finding that children who suffered many ordinary childhood infections were no less allergic than those who suffered few, whereas children exposed to diverse environmental microbes were, tests both halves of that contrast at once. The finding that children raised in unusually clean, nearly germ-free households had markedly higher rates of allergic disease is the trap: it fits the crude slogan equally well and never separates infection from symbiotic exposure. The claim about adults who contract frequent respiratory infections concerns adults and general immune strength, not childhood allergy. And the fact that the 'old friend' microorganisms were far more common in the human environments of thousands of years ago is consistent with the account but supplies no evidence about who develops allergies.
item.correct_answer: Children who suffered many ordinary childhood infections were no less allergic than those who suffered few, whereas children exposed to diverse environmental microbes were.

distractor_rationales.choice: Children raised in unusually clean, nearly germ-free households had markedly higher rates of allergic disease than did children who grew up in ordinary, less sanitized homes.
Adults who contract frequent respiratory infections tend to have weaker immune systems overall than adults who rarely fall ill.
The 'old friend' microorganisms were far more common in the human environments of thousands of years ago than they are in the households of modern industrialized countries today.
